newsitem.title: USA: N.Ireland Unionist calls for change in peace talks.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland Unionist calls for change in peace talks.

text.p: Northern Ireland Unionist leader David Trimble called for changes in U.S.-mediated peace talks, currently in recess, at a meeting on Thursday with a senior State Department official.

The inter-party talks, chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, were adjourned last week with the province's bitterly divided pro-British Protestant and pro-Irish Roman Catholics still split on the way forward.

"We reviewed the situation and looked forward to the resumption of (the) talks in June," Trimble said after meeting Under Secretary for Political Affairs Peter Tarnoff, who holds the No. 3 rank in the State Department.
"We expressed the view to him that we felt that there would need to be some changes in terms of the context or the way in which things are being done to avoid the present impasse," Trimble said.
"We felt that if we returned in June in exactly the same positions as we are at present then the process would have great difficulty in being continued."

Trimble gave no further details of the changes he wanted to see in the talks, which have been adjourned because of British general elections due by May 22. The Unionists are the leading Protestant party in Northern Ireland.
Currently excluded from the talks is Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army, because of the IRA's refusal to renew a ceasefire.
Irish politicians of various parties are arriving in Washington to attend a White House reception on next Monday marking St. Patrick's day.
Trimble met acting National Security Adviser Samuel Berger and deputy National Security Adviser James Steinberg at the White House after his visit to the State Department.

He said they had assured him the United States wanted to see the IRA renew its ceasefire in deed as well as word. He said he also sensed a U.S. frustration with the lack of progress in peace negotiations, but no lessening of the U.S. commitment to the talks.

Northern Ireland's John Hume, the leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, also met Berger at the White House on Thursday, saying afterwards that they discussed the prospects for restoring the ceasefire.
"I believe there is a very good chance of getting it restored," Hume told reporters. "I hope that we will succeed sooner rather than later."
